Saturday, 23 August 2031. Yves Le Goff, 87, has come from Nantes by train, with a crêpe pan in his suitcase. He’s in Odile’s kitchen on rue d’Austerlitz. Odile, very weak, watches him from her armchair.
There you are. The first galette. Buckwheat this time. No cassava. And no rum either.
You were the one who made the captain’s crêpe, in Brazil. Henri wrote to me about it. The captain was ill for two days.
It wasn’t the crêpe, it was the rum. But that’s a secret I’ll take to my grave.
(tastes) It’s delicious. What I like is the taste of the sea it has. Strange, for a crêpe.
It’s the salted butter. Me, I only make crêpes with salted butter. Henri said it was the only Breton thing he could stand.
Yves, tell me. What I don’t remember well is the first evening in Dakar. Was it you who recorded him?
Yes, it was me. He was on deck, alone. It’s the only time I saw him take out the harmonica in front of anyone. Well, he didn’t know I was there.
What makes me laugh is his voice at the end. “Yves, turn that thing off.” He was furious, wasn’t he?
Furious? He didn’t speak to me for a week. Then one evening he came to see me and said: “Keep it. One day someone will need it.” That’s why I never erased it.
(tears in her eyes) He knew. He always knew everything before everyone else.
So did you, Odile. You were the one who understood his hand, in Marseille. Nobody else had understood it. What he owed you, I don’t think you’ll ever know.
Yes, I do. I’ve known since April. It’s in his notebooks. In the passé simple. Do you want me to whistle you something, old sailor?
That’s exactly why I came. For the crêpe, and for that.
In “C’est TOI qui…” the stress falls on the highlighted word.
French can’t stress a word with the voice alone, as English can. It uses a construction: it puts the important element between “c’est” and “qui / que”:
C’est toi qui as fait la crêpe. (you, not someone else)
C’est le beurre salé que j’aime.
C’est à Marseille que je l’ai rencontré.
C’est en 1971 qu’ils se sont connus.
C’est pour ça que je suis venu.
After “c’est moi qui”, the verb agrees with “moi”: “C’est moi qui SUIS venu”, “C’est toi qui AS fait”, “C’est nous qui AVONS gagné”. The typical mistake: “c’est moi qui a” ✗.
2. Ce qui… c’est / ce que… c’est / ce dont… c’est
To announce an important element at the end of the sentence:
What I miss is his voice. (qui = subject of “manquer”)
What I like is the taste of the sea. (que = object of “aimer”)
What I remember is his laugh. (dont = “se souvenir DE”)
What I’m thinking of is her. (à quoi = “penser À”)
The choice of pronoun depends on the verb, as with relative clauses (ch. 39): verb + DE → ce dont; verb + À → ce à quoi.
In speech, the French move an element to the start (or end) of the sentence and pick it up with a pronoun:
Moi, je ne fais que des galettes.
Dislocation is VERY common in speech and sounds natural. In formal writing use “c’est… qui/que” instead.

Summer 2031 had been very hot in Lyon. Odile no longer left her flat. She spent her days in her armchair by the open window, facing Fourvière, with a fan Radu had put in for her and a glass of lemonade Isabelle refilled every hour. She read little. She slept a lot. But when she was awake, she was perfectly herself.

It was Rose-Hélène who came to wake her every morning at seven with her harmonica. She crossed the landing in her pyjamas, knocked three times on the door, as Odile had taught her, and went in without waiting for an answer. Then she blew the three notes, standing in the middle of the sitting room. Odile opened her eyes, smiled, and whistled the next three notes. It was their ritual. Nobody had the right to touch it.

Henri-Ion, who was seven months old, often spent his afternoons on Odile’s lap. He tried to grab her glasses, her necklaces, her white hair. She let him. She told him about the sea, the ships, a sailor who whistled. What she told him, nobody really knew. But Ioana had noticed that Henri-Ion never cried in Odile’s arms. Never.

Dr Martin came by every day, late in the morning. He hid nothing from Odile, because she would never have forgiven him. Her heart was tired. Her lungs too. There wasn’t much more to be done, except leave her in peace and ease her suffering. Odile had understood before he did. “Don’t worry, Martin,” she told him. “It’s not you who decides. It’s me. And I haven’t finished yet.”

What she hadn’t finished yet, everyone knew. She was waiting for a crêpe. Yves Le Goff had promised to come from Nantes as soon as his legs allowed. He was eighty-seven, with a bad hip. He had cancelled twice in July. Then, in mid-August, he phoned Julien. “I’m arriving on the 23rd,” he said. “With the pan. Whatever happens.”

On Saturday 23 August, Julien went to fetch him at Part-Dieu station. Yves got off the train slowly, leaning on his carved stick, with a small sailor’s bag on his shoulder. In the bag, wrapped in a tea towel, was an old cast-iron pan, black, heavy as an anchor. “It’s been round the world three times,” he explained. “It can manage Nantes to Lyon.”

He had also brought buckwheat flour bought from a Breton miller, salted butter, eggs from his neighbour and a bottle of cider. No rum. He had sworn. Julien helped him up the stairs on rue d’Austerlitz, step by step. On the first floor, Yves stopped in front of Odile’s door. He took off his cap. His hands were trembling a little.

They had never met. They had written several letters since March, they had spoken on the phone, but they had never met. And yet, when the door opened and Yves came into the sitting room, Odile held out her arms to him as to an old friend. “Here you are at last,” she said. “You’re sixty years late.” Yves laughed. Then he cried. Then they both laughed.

Yves settled into Odile’s little kitchen as into a cargo ship’s galley. He refused all help. He heated the pan, made the batter, and made the first galette with gestures his hands had known for seventy years. The smell of salted butter filled the whole flat, then the landing, then the stairwell. The neighbour on the third floor came down to ask what was going on.

Odile tasted the galette. She closed her eyes. She chewed for a long time, very slowly, the way you taste a rare wine. Then she said that what she liked was the taste of the sea. Yves explained it was the salted butter. Odile shook her head. “No,” she said. “It’s you. You’re the one who tastes of the sea. Like him.”

They talked all afternoon. About storms. About stopovers. About the captain’s crêpe in Brazil, and the rum that wasn’t in the crêpe. About the evening in Dakar, the cassette, Henri’s furious voice at the end of the recording. Yves told her what Henri had said a week later: “Keep it. One day someone will need it.” Odile wept silently.

Julien stayed in the corridor. He didn’t want to go in. What he heard through the half-open door didn’t belong to him. It was a conversation that had begun in 1971, on the deck of a cargo ship, and was ending sixty years later, in a sitting room in the Croix-Rousse, between two people who had loved the same man in two different ways.

Around six, Odile asked Yves if he wanted her to whistle him something. Yves answered that that was exactly why he had come. For the crêpe, and for that. So Odile whistled the waltz. Not just the third verse this time. The whole waltz, from beginning to end. Her voice was very weak. She stopped sometimes to breathe. But she went all the way to the end.

At the third verse, Yves began to whistle with her. He too whistled out of tune, like Henri, like Rose-Hélène, like everyone. They whistled the eight bars together, the old lady in her armchair and the old sailor by the window, facing Fourvière. In the corridor, Julien rested his head against the wall and closed his eyes.

That night Yves slept in Odile’s guest room, the one where Ioana’s grandmother had slept so many times. The next morning, when Rose-Hélène came with her harmonica, she found a stranger making crêpes in the kitchen. She looked at him warily, then asked if he could whistle. Yves whistled three notes. She adopted him on the spot.

Yves left on Sunday afternoon. Before leaving, he knelt, with difficulty, in front of Odile’s armchair and kissed her hand. “In the spring,” he said. “For the Lyon planting. Keep me a seat.” Odile smiled. “I’ll keep you the best one. In the front row. Next to me.” Neither of them believed what they were saying. But they said it anyway. That’s what people who love each other do.

The following week, Odile asked for writing paper and a pen. She spent several afternoons writing, slowly, often stopping to rest. Isabelle watched her without asking questions. She knew. Hélène had done the same thing two years earlier, before 3 May. There were people who left letters when they went, as others leave flowers.

On Sunday 31 August, it was cooler. For the first time in weeks, Odile asked to be taken outside. Radu and Julien carried her down in her wheelchair, step by step, with a thousand precautions. Isabelle pushed the wheelchair to the little square at the end of the street, under the plane trees. Rose-Hélène walked alongside, holding the hand of her grandmother of the heart.

They stayed there an hour, in the sun. Odile watched the children playing, the pigeons, the people passing by. She hardly spoke. At one point she said to Rose-Hélène: “Do you know what I like best in the waltz? The silence. The eight bars where nobody plays. That’s when you hear the ones who are no longer here.” Rose-Hélène nodded, as if she understood.

That evening the whole family had dinner at Odile’s, around her armchair. She wanted them all to be there: Isabelle, Ioana, Julien, the children, Radu and Lucia. She ate almost nothing. But she listened to each of them talk, smiling, the way you listen to music. Before dessert she asked Julien to open the window wide. She wanted to see the lights of Fourvière.

Around ten she said she was tired. Isabelle helped her to bed. Before turning out the light, Odile asked Rose-Hélène, who didn’t want to go to sleep, to play her the three notes. The little one blew into the harmonica, very softly. Odile whistled the next three. Then she said: “Good night, my darling. Tomorrow, you wake me up.”

Odile passed away during the night, peacefully, in her sleep. Isabelle, sleeping in the armchair beside the bed, noticed nothing. She woke at five in the morning and understood at once, from the silence. The window was still open. The lights of Fourvière had gone out too. The sky was beginning to pale above the hill.

On the bedside table, next to Yves’s postcard, the dried lime branch and the photo of Henri as a sailor, there was a pile of envelopes. One for Isabelle. One for Julien. One for Ioana. One for Radu and Lucia. One for Yves. One for Amina, which surprised everyone very much. And a last one, thicker than the others, on which was written: “For Rose-Hélène. For later.”

At seven, as every morning, Rose-Hélène crossed the landing in her pyjamas, harmonica in hand. Ioana tried to stop her. She didn’t know how to explain. But Rose-Hélène had already knocked three times on the door. Isabelle opened it. Her eyes were red. She crouched down in front of the little girl and took her in her arms without a word.

Rose-Hélène looked over Isabelle’s shoulder, towards the empty armchair by the window. She was three and a half. She didn’t understand what death was. But she had understood that nobody would whistle the next three notes that morning. She thought for a long time, very serious. Then she raised the harmonica to her lips and played the three notes anyway, towards the empty armchair.

Then, on her own, she whistled the next three. Odile’s. Out of tune, with lots of breath. But she whistled them. Isabelle burst into sobs. Ioana, on the landing, began to cry too. Julien, holding Henri-Ion in his arms, stood motionless in the doorway. He had just understood that the waltz had passed into other hands.

The farewell took place on Saturday 6 September, in the Hélène Morel hall, at La Duchère. Odile had asked for it, in her letter to Isabelle. No church, no speeches, no flowers. Only music, children, and the lime tree by the door. The hall was full. There were people standing all the way out into the street.

Yves Le Goff had come back from Nantes, despite his hip, despite the journey, despite everything. Mr Benhamou had come from Marseille with three children from L’Estaque. Mrs Vandamme from Lille, with her father’s cornet. Antoine had sent from Corsica a branch of the lime tree he had planted in June. Catherine Dumas was there, and Olivier Marchand, and Bernard Delorme, and Mrs Roux in her wheelchair.

There were no speeches. Only music. The La Duchère orchestra, conducted by Théo, played the Brahms dance, then Lucia’s Spanish tune, then the “Waltz for two women” Julien had composed for Hélène and Odile three years earlier. And to finish, Henri’s waltz. Inès began alone, on Lucien Roux’s clarinet. Then the whole orchestra.

At the third verse, as always, the orchestra fell silent. Eight bars of silence. Odile’s place. In the hall, nobody moved. Everyone was looking at the front row, where an armchair had been left empty, with a blue shawl on it. The silence lasted. One bar. Two bars. Nobody dared breathe.

Then, from the front row, a little voice rose. Rose-Hélène had stood up from her chair, beside the empty armchair. She was whistling. Out of tune, with lots of breath, stopping now and then to take a breath. But she whistled the eight bars. Odile’s eight bars. She had learned them on her own, during the summer, every morning, on the landing.

In the middle of the fifth bar, another voice joined hers. It was Yves, in the third row, whistling with her. Then Isabelle. Then Julien. Then Mrs Roux, Mr Benhamou, Théo, Lucia, Radu, Ioana. Then the whole hall. Three hundred people whistling out of tune, together, the eight bars of an old lady who was no longer there to whistle them.

When the orchestra came back in at the ninth bar, Théo was crying as he conducted. Inès was crying as she played. Nobody had ever heard the waltz played as it was that day. Later, Mr Benhamou would say it was the most beautiful concert of his life, and he had played in the greatest jazz clubs in Paris.

After the music, Mrs Roux asked to be wheeled to the lime tree by the door. She hung on a low branch Lucien’s old clarinet reed, the one she had given Odile for her eightieth birthday. “She gave it back to me last week,” she explained. “She told me: ‘Keep it for the tree. It will know how to wait.’” Nobody understood what she meant. But everyone nodded.

Odile had asked, in her letter, for her ashes to be scattered at sea, off Marseille, where Henri had dropped anchor on 3 June 1971. Isabelle would do it in the spring, with Yves, on a little fishing boat Mr Benhamou knew. But she had also asked for one other thing: a handful of ashes at the foot of the La Duchère lime tree. “To be near the children,” she had written. “And near Hélène. We still have things to say to each other, she and I.”

The letter for Julien was very short. He read it that same evening, alone, in the kitchen, in front of the calendar. “My dear little Julien. Don’t worry. It isn’t me who has left. It’s the waltz that goes on. Leave your door open. And if one day you hear whistling across the landing, don’t look for who it is. Answer. Your old neighbour, Odile.”

The letter for Amina contained a single sentence, written in large letters: “Emotions are facts too.” Amina read it at the office on Monday morning. She framed it and hung it above her computer, next to the map of France with its twelve pins. She said nothing to Julien. But that day, for the first time, she closed her office door to cry.

Isabelle gave Yves his letter at the station, before he left for Nantes. He didn’t open it in front of her. He read it on the train, between Lyon and Moulins, and called Isabelle when he got home that evening, in a voice that trembled. Odile had written: “Thank you for the crêpe. It was the best. And thank you for keeping him alive. Now it’s your turn to be waited for. Don’t hurry.”

Isabelle decided to keep her mother’s flat on rue d’Austerlitz. She didn’t want to live there. She just wanted it to stay there, across the landing, with the armchair by the window and the view of Fourvière. “For the children,” she explained to Ioana. “So they always have a door opposite to open.” She gave a spare set of keys to Rose-Hélène, tied to a blue ribbon.

On Wednesday 10 September, at seven in the morning, Rose-Hélène crossed the landing in her pyjamas, as every morning. She opened the door opposite with her blue-ribbon key. The sitting room was empty. The armchair was waiting by the window, facing Fourvière, with the blue shawl draped over the back. Rose-Hélène planted herself in the middle of the room, very straight, like a little conductor.

She blew the three notes on Henri’s harmonica. Then she whistled the next three, Odile’s. And across the landing, through the open door, Julien answered, whistling the three after that, as Odile had asked him to. Then Ioana. Then, in his mother’s arms, Henri-Ion let out a little cry, high and joyful, that sounded like nothing anyone knew. It was his first note.

Outside, on the hill of Fourvière, the sun was rising. All over France, in twelve towns, twelve little lime trees were beginning to lose their first leaves. They would flower again in June. They would flower every year, long after everyone had forgotten who Henri was, who Hélène was, who Odile was. But somewhere there would always be a child to whistle three notes. And someone, on the other side of a door, to answer.

At the end of August, Julien writes Yves a letter of thanks. Listen to the text twice, then read it aloud. At the end you answer 4 questions.
Dear Yves, it is with great emotion that I write to you. What you did for Odile last Saturday, I will never forget. It wasn’t just a crêpe you brought her. It was a piece of her youth.

What moved me most was the moment when you whistled together, she in her armchair, you by the window. I was in the corridor. I didn’t dare come in. I didn’t want to interrupt a conversation that had begun in 1971.

Odile told me that evening that it was the best crêpe she had ever eaten. She told me something else too. It was you, she said, who kept Henri alive all those years, without knowing it. With a cassette and a tape recorder.
What she needs most now is calm. She is very tired. Dr Martin comes every day. But she smiles a lot, and she still whistles in the morning when Rose-Hélène opens her door.

It is you I am thinking of as I write these lines, and Henri, and all the sailors who waited for someone. You kept your word. You came before it was too late. That is something few people know how to do.

Come back in the spring, for the Lyon planting. Odile has kept you a seat in the front row. And if by any chance she can’t be there, it will be Rose-Hélène who whistles her part. She’s already practising. With all my friendship, Julien.
